New York City, US — Aryna Sabalenka of Belarus serves to Czechia’s Linda Nosková during the women’s quarter-final at the US Open in Flushing Meadows. There has been little evidence of vulnerability from Sabalenka during the tournament. She swept through Camila Osorio, Polina Iatcenko, Kamilla Rakhimova and Taylor Townsend without dropping a set before surviving her first serious examination against the Wimbledon champion Nosková in Tuesday’s quarter-final, coming through 7-6, 3-6, 7-6 after 2 hours and 22 minutes. — Photograph: Al Bello/Getty Images

Source: The Guardian — Photos of the Day

item.source: The Atlantic — Photography
item.description:
© Lana Tannir / Ocean Photographer of the Year — Finalist, Conservation Hope. Animal care workers perform daily physiotherapy on Norah, a juvenile harbour porpoise undergoing rehabilitation at SOS Dolfijn in the Netherlands. Rescued after being stranded on the Dutch coast, Norah was treated for multiple serious conditions, including pneumonia and severe muscle spasms. This image captures the intensive care required to return her to the sea.

item.title: [The Atlantic — Photography] Winners of Ocean Photographer of the Year 2026
item.source: The Atlantic — Photography
item.description:
© Mitsuna Kawai / Ocean Photographer of the Year — First Place, Ocean Unseen. A ribbonfish rises vertically through the dark waters of Osezaki, Japan. Its long, silver body and delicate fins are adapted for life in the open ocean. This image was captured during a winter blackwater dive. Around the ribbonfish, a swarm of salps—small jelly-like animals that feed on tiny particles in the ocean—provides a glimpse of life moving through the deep sea.

Source: The Atlantic — Photography

item.title: [The Atlantic — Photography] Winners of Ocean Photographer of the Year 2026
item.source: The Atlantic — Photography
item.description:
© Chen Lin / Ocean Photographer of the Year — Finalist, Human Connection. From above, moored fishing and tourist boats bloom across the sapphire-blue sea, like the petals of a flower. Fringed by golden coastal vegetation, the shoreline becomes an abstract pattern that is diﬃcult to recognize from ground level.

Source: The Atlantic — Photography

item.title: [The Atlantic — Photography] Winners of Ocean Photographer of the Year 2026
item.source: The Atlantic — Photography
item.description:
© Daniel Taylor / Ocean Photographer of the Year — Finalist, Conservation Impact. A silky shark circles helplessly after taking bait from an illegal longline, its fate sealed by a steel hook and heavy line designed to prevent escape. Photographed less than 48 hours after Baja California’s seasonal shark-fishing ban ended, the image reveals a hidden reality unfolding far from shore. A small group of pilot fish remains beside the shark, highlighting how the loss of one animal can ripple throughout an entire ecosystem.

Source: The Atlantic — Photography

item.title: [The Atlantic — Photography] Winners of Ocean Photographer of the Year 2026
item.source: The Atlantic — Photography
item.description:
© Iris Uijttewaal / Ocean Photographer of the Year — Finalist, Ocean Unseen. A pygmy seahorse, no larger than a grain of rice, clings to a delicate hydroid in the reefs of Raja Ampat, Indonesia. Perfectly camouflaged, these tiny animals are rarely seen, even by experienced divers.

Source: The Atlantic — Photography

item.title: [The Atlantic — Photography] Winners of Ocean Photographer of the Year 2026
item.source: The Atlantic — Photography
item.description:
© Yuta Shigeno / Ocean Photographer of the Year — Third Place, Conservation Hope. A male white-spotted puﬀerfish creates an intricate spawning nest in the sand. The fish carefully shapes a two-meter-wide radial pattern using only his fins. Built over several days, this structure and its subtle details reveal the extraordinary eﬀort this small fish invests in reproduction.

Source: The Atlantic — Photography

item.title: [The Atlantic — Photography] Winners of Ocean Photographer of the Year 2026
item.source: The Atlantic — Photography
item.description:
© James Ferrara / Ocean Photographer of the Year — First Place, Conservation Impact. A whale shark is surrounded by divers and snorkelers in the Maldives, revealing the overwhelming pressure that crowded wildlife tourism can place on marine animals. With almost 50 people visible in the frame, this image captures the reality behind some popular wildlife encounters: an animal seeking space while people compete for a closer view. It challenges us to rethink how we experience and protect the species we admire.

Source: The Atlantic — Photography

item.title: [The Atlantic — Photography] Winners of Ocean Photographer of the Year 2026

c© Thomas Pavy / Ocean Photographer of the Year — First Place, Conservation Hope. A great hammerhead shark, known as Tamataroa in French Polynesia, is photographed at 55 meters depth in Tiputa Pass, Rangiroa Atoll, during a population survey. This image represents the moment an anonymous shark becomes a known individual. Through photo identification and laser-calibrated video photogrammetry, scientists can track sharks over time to measure their size, sex, and population trends.
